draft.title: The binomial distribution
card: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes, success or failure. The chance of success is p, and the chance of failure is 1 − p.
Let X be the number of successes in n trials. X is binomial if n is fixed, the trials are independent and p is the same every time. We write X ~ Bin(n, p).
The chance of exactly x successes is Pr(X = x) = nCx × p^x × (1 − p)^(n − x). Here nCx counts the ways to place x successes among n trials.
Example: a fair coin is tossed 3 times and X is the number of heads. X ~ Bin(3, 0.5). Pr(X = 2) = 3 × 0.5² × 0.5 = 0.375.
draft.remember: Fixed n, independent trials, same p each time: count the successes and you have a binomial.

a.q: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. X is the number of heads. What is Pr(X = 3)?
a.why: X ~ Bin(4, 0.5), so Pr(X = 3) = 4 × 0.5³ × 0.5 = 4 × 0.0625 = 0.25. The option 0.0625 leaves out the factor 4 for the ways to place the 3 heads.
a.clue: Count the ways to place 3 heads among 4 tosses.

b.q: Which situation is best modelled by a binomial distribution?
opts: Number of sixes in 10 rolls of a fair die
Number of rolls of a fair die until the first six
Number of red cards in 5 cards dealt, no replacing
Number of rolls of a die until 3 sixes appear
b.why: Ten rolls give a fixed n, independent trials and the same p of 1/6 each time. Dealing cards without replacement changes the chance of red after each card, so the trials are not independent and p does not stay the same.
b.clue: Check for a fixed number of trials and a constant p.

b.best: Number of sixes in 10 rolls of a fair die
